title: Mycoplasma Pneumoniae
subject: Medicine
summary: A common cause of atypical pneumonia in young adults, especially in low‑resource settings. Diagnosis relies on clinical features, serology or PCR when available, and treatment is with macrolides or tetracyclines.

sections.p: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a small, wall‑less bacterium that colonises the respiratory tract and causes an atypical pneumonia characterised by a dry cough and gradual onset.
b: Requires specialised culture or molecular methods

t.b: Detects recent infection; a rise in titres confirms diagnosis

t.a: PCR of sputum or nasopharyngeal swab
t.b: Direct detection of bacterial DNA; most sensitive when performed early

sections.p: Most cases are mild to moderate. Severe disease is defined by hypoxaemia (SpO2 <90% on room air), respiratory distress, or need for supplemental oxygen.
b: Mild: cough, low‑grade fever, no dyspnoea

sections.p: Primary infection in adolescents and young adults; secondary infection in immunocompromised hosts.
b: Close contact in schools or dormitories

t.b: Increases risk of severe disease and complications

sections.p: Gradual onset of dry cough, low‑grade fever, headache, myalgia, and sometimes wheeze or asthma exacerbation.

t.b: Diffuse crackles or wheeze; no lobar consolidation

sections.p: Investigations are limited in low‑resource settings; focus on clinical assessment and basic labs.

t.b: Normal or mild infiltrates in early disease
Elevated but less than bacterial pneumonia; helps rule out severe bacterial infection

sections.p: Complications are uncommon but can be serious.

t.b: <90% indicates need for oxygen and possible ICU referral

sections.p: Treat with a macrolide or tetracycline; supportive care and monitoring of oxygenation.
b: Monitor for relapse or secondary infection

sections.p: Re‑evaluate if symptoms persist >10 days or worsen; advise vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce co‑infection.

sections.p: Serology may be negative early; PCR may be unavailable; chest X‑ray can be normal in early disease.
b: Normal X‑ray does not exclude infection

whenToSeekHelp: Failure to improve after 5 days of therapy

faq.q: Why is a macrolide preferred over a fluoroquinolone?
faq.a: Macrolides are effective, have a good safety profile in children and pregnancy, and avoid tendon toxicity seen with fluoroquinolones.

faq.q: Can I treat a mild case with only supportive care?
faq.a: If the patient is stable, no hypoxaemia, and has no comorbidities, observation with antipyretics is acceptable, but most guidelines recommend a short course of macrolide.

faq.q: What if the patient is HIV positive?
faq.a: They are at higher risk of severe disease; consider early oxygen, monitor closely, and use macrolide or tetracycline depending on age and pregnancy status.

exam: A 17‑year‑old presents with a 10‑day dry cough and low‑grade fever. Chest X‑ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. What is the most appropriate first‑line treatment? — Macrolide (azithromycin) because it covers M. pneumoniae and is safe in adolescents.

A 25‑year‑old with HIV on ART develops a dry cough and SpO2 88% on room air. What is the next step? — Start supplemental oxygen and give a macrolide; consider adding a second antibiotic if bacterial co‑infection is suspected.
A 6‑year‑old boy has a 7‑day cough and mild fever. Chest X‑ray is normal. Which investigation is most useful? — Serology for IgM/IgG; PCR is less available in low‑resource settings.
A patient improves after 3 days of azithromycin but cough persists. What should you do? — Re‑evaluate for secondary bacterial pneumonia; consider adding a β‑lactam if clinical deterioration.
Why is doxycycline avoided in children under 8? — It can cause permanent teeth discoloration and affect bone growth.

A patient with a history of asthma develops wheeze and cough after a viral illness. How can you differentiate M. pneumoniae from a viral exacerbation? — Look for gradual onset, low‑grade fever, and interstitial infiltrates; viral exacerbations usually have higher fever and rapid onset.
